text.en: Imagine you are in bed and you hear a noise that should not be there. What would you do? Would you panic, or would you think of a clever plan? This comic story, from Amar Chitra Katha, shows a husband and wife who use their wits to catch a thief.

To rescue means to save someone from danger. The book asks who rescues us in trouble, such as firefighters, doctors and the police. The policeman in the story is the village kotwal. Some people say thaanedar. In your own language there is another word. The book also asks what you would do if you were alone and faced a problem: give up, feel angry, or think quickly about ways to solve it. Thinking quickly is the best choice, and the story shows it.
The story is set in a village at night. The main characters are the husband and wife, and the kotwal named Rama. Other characters are the thief who enters the house. The problem is a thief who gets into the house, and the solution is a clever trick that brings the kotwal. The story is told as a comic with speech balloons, so the lines of talk carry the story.
At the end of a hard day the man and his wife are very sleepy, and they lie down to rest. Then the wife hears a noise and asks the husband to be quiet and listen. He realises somebody is trying to get in. The noise stops, and they think the person has got inside. The man guesses it is a thief who must have somehow got past Rama, the kotwal.
The husband whispers a plan to his wife. They will pretend to talk to each other, while the thief listens. Inside, the thief thinks: they are awake, and I will have to wait until they fall asleep. I wonder where they keep their money. The couple start chatting about what to name their child. If it is a boy, they will call him Rama. The man says that when the boy is in the house he will call softly, if he is in the yard a little louder, and if he is in the street very loudly. The thief thinks they are talking about their money.
The thief gets bored of the silly game and hopes they will stop and fall asleep. The husband then begins to call out the name Rama, first softly, then louder, and then very loudly. Rama, the village kotwal, hears his name and runs to the house from which the call came. He finds that a thief has dug his way into the house. The thief is caught and taken to the kotwal. The villagers help, and the couple can sleep. The story shows that cleverness can solve problems.
A contraction is a short form of two words with an apostrophe in place of the missing letters. I am becomes I'm, it is becomes it's, and they are becomes they're. Other examples are what's for what is, I'll for I will, I'd for I would, we'll for we will, that's for that is, we're for we are, don't for do not, you'll for you will and must've for must have. We use the contracted form while speaking and the expanded form in formal writing.
The present progressive tense tells what is going on at the moment of speaking. It uses am, is or are plus the verb with ing, such as I am studying, my friend is reading, we are playing. Adverbs give more information about a verb, such as how, when or where. In the story, closely, softly and loudly tell how the man listens and calls. Examples with other adverbs: he solved the problem quickly, she danced gracefully, the musician played beautifully. Notice that most adverbs of manner are formed by adding ly to an adjective.
An exclamatory sentence shows a strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark, such as: Wow, what an intelligent man he is! An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark, such as: What is your favourite story? In the story, hum! What a hard day it has been! shows tiredness, and Ah, at last they've stopped their chatter! shows relief. The book also teaches safety: lock doors and windows at night, do not talk to strangers, report anything unusual and dial 100 in an emergency.

problem.en: Make the sentence in the present progressive: I (study) in Grade 6.

text.en: Check the subject: I takes am.

why.en: I goes with am in the present progressive.

text.en: Add ing to the verb: study becomes studying, so the sentence is I am studying in Grade 6.

problem.en: Expand the contraction they're and use it in a sentence.

text.en: The apostrophe replaces the letter a, so they're is they are.

why.en: Contractions drop letters, and the apostrophe marks the spot.

text.en: Sentence: They're playing in the yard, which means they are playing in the yard.

why.en: The sentence uses the present progressive too.

problem.en: Punctuate and name the type: Oh how big the hole is

text.en: The sentence shows surprise, so it is exclamatory.

why.en: Strong feeling means an exclamatory sentence.

text.en: Write it as Oh, how big the hole is! with an exclamation mark.

why.en: The end mark matches the type of sentence.

prompt.en: Tell the story in your own words: how did the man and wife get the kotwal to catch the thief?

requiredIdeas.en: The couple heard a thief enter.
They pretended to talk about naming a child Rama.
They called out Rama louder and louder.
The kotwal named Rama came and caught the thief.

commonMisconceptions.en: The kotwal was already inside the house.
The thief was caught by the wife alone.

points.en: Rama to the Rescue is a comic about a clever couple and a thief.
They use the name of the kotwal, Rama, to call for help without frightening the thief.
The solution came from calm and quick thinking.
Contractions like I'll, don't and we're are short forms with an apostrophe.
Present progressive tense uses am, is or are with the verb plus ing.
Adverbs tell how, when or where, and exclamatory sentences show strong feeling.
